lessons.title: Finding and Vetting Brand Partners
lessons.body: Start by identifying brands that already align with your content and audience. In Africa, local brands like Dangote, MTN, or Jumia often have influencer budgets, but so do smaller D2C startups in Lagos, Nairobi, or Cape Town. Use tools like BuzzSumo or native Instagram/TikTok search to see who is already working with influencers in your niche. Also check African influencer marketing platforms like Hari and Waya, which connect creators with brands. Once you have a list, vet each brand: look at their recent campaigns, engagement rates on their own social posts, and whether they have a history of paying influencers on time. Ask in creator WhatsApp groups or on Twitter (X) using hashtags like #AfricanCreators to get honest feedback. Red flags include brands that ask for free content 'for exposure', have no clear product, or refuse to sign a simple contract. Always check if the brand's values match yoursâif you promote a betting app and your audience is young students, you could lose trust. A good vetting method is to request a 15-minute discovery call before agreeing to anything. Ask about their budget range, timeline, and what success looks like. If they dodge these questions, walk away. Remember, your reputation is your biggest asset. In Africa, word travels fast in tight-knit creator communities, so a bad partnership can cost you future deals. Start with smaller local brands to build a track record, then approach bigger names. Keep a simple spreadsheet with columns: brand name, contact person, rate offered, deliverables, payment terms, and notes. This helps you compare and negotiate from a position of knowledge.

lessons.title: Crafting a Winning Pitch Deck
lessons.body: Your pitch deck is your handshake before you meet. Keep it to 8-10 slides, mobile-friendly, and under 5MB so it can be sent via WhatsApp or email. Slide 1: Your name, handle, and a one-line value proposition like 'I help Kenyan youth discover fintech apps.' Slide 2: Your audience demographicsâage, location, gender, and top 3 cities. Use real data from Instagram Insights or TikTok Analytics. Slide 3: Engagement metricsâaverage views, likes, comments, shares, and save rate. Show a 30-day trend, not just one viral post. Slide 4: Your content styleâinclude 3-4 screenshots of your best posts that match the brand's vibe. Slide 5: Case studiesâpick 2-3 past brand partnerships, show the results (e.g., 'Drove 500 app installs in 2 weeks for X brand'). Slide 6: Your proposed deliverablesâe.g., 1 Instagram Reel, 2 Stories with swipe-up, and 1 TikTok video. Slide 7: Your rate card (see Lesson 3) with a clear package price. Slide 8: Testimonials from past brands or clients. Slide 9: Contact details and a call to action. Use Canva or Google Slides to design it; keep colors and fonts consistent with your personal brand. For African brands, include local contextâmention if your audience is in Nigeria, Ghana, or South Africa, and use local currency (NGN, GHS, ZAR) alongside USD. Always send the deck as a PDF to avoid formatting issues. Personalize each deck: change the brand name and reference a recent campaign they ran. This shows you did your homework. Finally, practice a 2-minute verbal pitch that summarizes the deck. You'll often need to pitch in a WhatsApp voice note or a quick call. Keep it confident and concise.

lessons.title: Understanding Rate Cards and Deliverables
lessons.body: A rate card is a public or private list of your prices for different services. It stops you from undervaluing yourself and speeds up negotiations. Start by calculating your baseline: how much time does one Instagram Reel take? If it's 4 hours and you want to earn $25 per hour, that's $100 minimum. But your rate should also reflect your reach and engagement. A common formula in Africa: for every 10,000 followers, charge $50-$150 per post, depending on niche and platform. For example, a Nigerian fashion influencer with 50k followers might charge â¦150,000 ($200) for a single feed post. Your rate card should list deliverables separately: Instagram Story (1 frame) â $50; Instagram Reel â $150; TikTok video â $120; YouTube integration â $300; bundle deals (3 posts + 2 stories) â 15% discount. Always add a line for usage rights: if the brand wants to run your content as a paid ad for 3 months, add 50% to the base rate. Exclusivity: if they don't want you working with competitors for 30 days, add 30%. Payment terms: 50% upfront, 50% on delivery, or 100% upfront for new brands. In Africa, mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo) is common, but for international brands, use Payoneer, Wise, or PayPal. Always invoice with your name, date, deliverables, amount, and payment details. Never start work without a signed agreement or at least a written confirmation via email or WhatsApp. If a brand asks for 'product only' deals, calculate the product's retail value and decide if it's worth your time. For example, a $50 skincare set for a 4-hour video is not worth it if your cash rate is $200. Stick to your rate card, but be open to negotiating the package, not the price per deliverable.

lessons.title: Negotiation Tactics for Higher Rates
lessons.body: Negotiation is not about being aggressive; it's about finding a win-win. First, never accept the first offer. If a brand offers $100 for a Reel, counter with $150 and justify it: 'My average Reel reaches 20,000 views, and my audience is 70% in Lagos, which matches your target.' Use silence as a toolâafter you state your rate, wait for their response. In African cultures, relationship-building matters, so start with a friendly tone, then get to business. If they say the budget is fixed, ask for non-cash value: extra product, a longer contract, or a shoutout on their page. Another tactic is the 'good, better, best' package: offer three optionsâbasic (1 post), standard (3 posts + 2 stories), premium (5 posts + 5 stories + usage rights). Price the middle option as your target, and make the premium look like a steal. If they still push back, ask: 'What budget can you work with?' Then see if you can reduce deliverables to match. For example, if they only have $80, offer one Story instead of a Reel. Always anchor high: if your ideal rate is $200, start at $250. This gives you room to 'concede' to $200. For repeat clients, offer a loyalty discount of 10% if they book 3 campaigns upfront. In Africa, many brands are new to influencer marketing, so educate them on the value: show a case study where your post drove sales. Use a negotiation script: 'I'm excited to work with you. Based on my engagement and the deliverables, my rate is $X. I can offer a 10% discount if we sign today.' Never negotiate against yourselfâdon't lower your price without getting something in return, like extra usage rights or a longer timeline. Finally, be prepared to walk away. If the rate is below your minimum, politely decline and suggest they check back when their budget grows.

lessons.title: Contracts: Exclusivity, Usage Rights, and Morality Clauses
lessons.body: A contract protects both you and the brand. Never work without one, even for a small deal. Key clauses to watch: Exclusivityâthis means you cannot work with competing brands for a set period. For example, if you promote a telco like MTN, they might ask you not to promote Airtel for 60 days. That's fine, but it should come with a higher fee (usually 20-50% more) because you're limiting your income. Usage rightsâthis is how long the brand can use your content and where. A common ask is 'perpetual usage worldwide'âthat means they can use your face in ads forever, anywhere. That should cost 2-3 times your base rate. Better to limit usage to 6 months, specific platforms, and specific regions (e.g., Nigeria only). Morality clauseâthis says you won't do anything that embarrasses the brand, like posting offensive content or getting into public scandals. It's standard, but make sure it's mutual: the brand shouldn't be able to cancel payment if you post something they disagree with politically. Also check for payment terms: net 30 means they pay 30 days after invoice. For African creators, net 7 or 14 is better. Include a late fee of 5% per week if they delay. Always get a signed contract via email or a digital signature tool like DocuSign. If a brand sends a 20-page contract, read it carefullyâor ask a lawyer friend to review. In many African countries, verbal agreements are hard to enforce, so written is key. Finally, keep a copy of every contract and invoice. If a brand breaches the contract, you can use it as evidence in small claims court or to warn other creators.

lessons.title: Managing Brand Relationships for Repeat Business
lessons.body: Getting a brand deal is hard; keeping the client is where the real money is. After you deliver, send a thank-you message within 24 hours and include a short performance report: views, engagement, clicks, and any sales data you can get. Use a simple Google Sheet or a PDF with screenshots. This shows you're professional and results-oriented. Ask for feedback: 'What did you like? What could I improve?' Then implement it next time. Set a reminder to check in with the brand every 4-6 weeksânot to pitch, but to share something useful: a new trend in their industry, a relevant article, or a quick note that you loved their latest campaign. This keeps you top of mind. Offer a loyalty program: after 3 campaigns, give a 10% discount or a free extra Story. For African brands, relationship is everythingâremember names, ask about their family, and be genuinely interested. If you're in the same city, suggest a coffee meeting. Also, ask for referrals: 'Do you know any other brands that might need my services?' Most of your future deals will come from happy clients. When you get a repeat deal, always send a fresh contract and invoiceâdon't assume the old terms apply. If the brand grows, your rates should grow too. After 6 months, politely raise your rates by 15-20% for new campaigns. If they value you, they'll pay. Finally, don't burn bridges. Even if a campaign didn't go well, stay polite and professional. The African influencer market is small, and word gets around. A brand you part with today might be your biggest client tomorrow.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Negotiating Brand Partnerships

This practical reference is the working toolkit for African creators and influencer managers who need to move from âwe got a DM from a brandâ to a signed, profitable, repeatable partnership. It assumes you already have an audience and a niche. The goal is to help you price, pitch, protect, and renew brand deals with the discipline of a small business â because that is what you are.

Across Africa, brand budgets are moving online fast. In Kenya, digital advertising spend has been growing at double-digit rates, with influencers increasingly included in campaign line items. In Nigeria, the creator economy is one of the fastest-growing segments of the media sector. In South Africa, brands routinely allocate 10â20% of campaign budgets to influencer activations. The opportunity is real. The risk is also real: vague briefs, delayed payments, unlimited usage rights, and exclusivity clauses that lock you out of your own category.

Use this reference as a checklist before every negotiation. It is organised around the six lessons in this module, with practical numbers, red flags, and templates you can adapt to your market.

1. Finding and Vetting Brand Partners

Not every brand deserves your audience. Vet for three things: budget, fit, and reputation. A brand with no influencer budget will waste your time. A brand that does not fit your niche will confuse your audience and reduce engagement. A brand with a bad payment reputation will cost you money.

In African markets, verify locally. Check whether the company is registered with the relevant authority â for example, the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC) in South Africa, the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) in Nigeria, or the Business Registration Service in Kenya. Ask for a purchase order or contract before you deliver. If a brand refuses paperwork, treat that as a signal.

2. Crafting a Winning Pitch Deck

Your pitch deck is a sales document, not a portfolio. It must answer the brandâs question: âWhat will I get for my money?â Keep it to 8â12 slides. In African markets, where brand managers are often juggling multiple campaigns with small teams, clarity beats creativity.

Include: a one-line positioning statement, audience demographics (age, gender, location, income where available), engagement metrics with screenshots, three case studies with results, your rate card summary, and a clear call to action. Use local data. If your audience is 60% Nigerian women aged 18â34 in Lagos and Abuja, say that. Brands pay for specificity.

3. Understanding Rate Cards and Deliverables

A rate card is your price list. It should cover content type, usage rights, exclusivity, and timeline. Below is a practical benchmark table for African markets. These are indicative ranges for mid-tier creators (10kâ100k followers) in 2024. Adjust for your niche, engagement rate, and production quality.

Table 1: Indicative influencer rate benchmarks in selected African markets (2024)
Deliverable Kenya (KES) Nigeria (NGN) South Africa (ZAR)
1 Instagram feed post 15,000â40,000 80,000â250,000 2,500â7,000
1 Instagram Story set (3â5 frames) 8,000â20,000 40,000â120,000 1,200â3,500
1 TikTok video 12,000â35,000 70,000â200,000 2,000â6,000
1 YouTube integration (60â90 sec) 40,000â120,000 250,000â700,000 7,000â20,000
Usage rights (30 days, paid ads) +20â50% +20â50% +20â50%
Exclusivity (30 days, category) +30â100% +30â100% +30â100%

Sources: Aggregated from Kenyan, Nigerian, and South African creator community rate surveys (2023â2024), including publicly shared rate cards from influencer agencies and the African Influencer Marketing Report (2023). Ranges vary by engagement rate, niche, and negotiation.

Deliverables must be specific. âTwo postsâ is not a deliverable. âOne Instagram Reel (15â30 seconds) posted between 1â7 March, one Instagram Story set of 5 frames within 24 hours of Reel, with swipe-up link, plus 30 days paid usage rightsâ is a deliverable.

4. Negotiation Tactics for Higher Rates

Negotiation is not confrontation. It is problem-solving. The brand has a budget and a goal. You have an audience and a skill. Your job is to find the overlap that pays you fairly.

Anchor high, but justify. If your rate card says KES 40,000 for a feed post, do not open at 40,000 if you expect to be negotiated down. Open at 50,000 and explain the value: engagement rate, audience quality, content production cost, and usage rights.

Bundle, donât discount. If the brand cannot meet your rate, offer a bundle: âI cannot do one post for 20,000, but I can do one post plus three Stories for 35,000.â This protects your rate card and gives the brand more value.

Charge for rights. Usage rights are a separate line item. If the brand wants to run your content as a paid ad for 90 days, that is not included in the post fee. It is a licence. Price it.

Know your walk-away number. Before the call, write down the lowest number you will accept. If the brand goes below it, politely decline. A bad deal costs you more than no deal â it sets a precedent for future negotiations.

5. Contracts: Exclusivity, Usage Rights, and Morality Clauses

Contracts protect both sides. In African markets, many deals are still done over WhatsApp and email. That is a risk. Insist on a written agreement, even a simple one-page contract, before you deliver.

Exclusivity. This means you cannot work with competing brands for a period. It is valuable to the brand and costly to you. Price it accordingly. A 30-day exclusivity clause in a narrow category (e.g., âmobile money apps in Kenyaâ) is worth 30â100% of your base fee. A 12-month exclusivity clause across all financial services is a red flag â it can lock you out of your entire income stream.

Usage rights. This is the brandâs right to use your content. Specify: where (organic social, paid ads, website, TV), for how long (30, 60, 90 days), and in which territories (Kenya only, or global). Unlimited, perpetual, worldwide usage rights should be priced at 2â5x your base fee, or refused.

Morality clauses. These allow the brand to terminate the contract if you do something that damages their reputation. They are standard, but they must be mutual and specific. A vague âconduct unbecomingâ clause is dangerous. Ask for a clear definition and a cure period.

â ï¸ RED WARNING: Never sign unlimited, perpetual, worldwide usage rights without a separate licence fee.

Some brands â especially in fintech, betting, and alcohol â will ask for âall rights in perpetuityâ in the first draft. This means they can use your face and content forever, anywhere, without paying you again. In several African markets, creators have lost control of their content this way. If the brand insists, either price it at 3â5x your base fee or walk away. Also beware of exclusivity clauses that block you from your entire category for more than 90 days. Read every line. If you do not understand it, get a lawyer or a trusted manager to review it.

6. Managing Brand Relationships for Repeat Business

The first deal is a test. The second deal is the business. To turn one campaign into a retainer, you must deliver on time, communicate proactively, and report results.

Send a post-campaign report within 72 hours of the campaign ending. Include reach, impressions, engagement rate, clicks, and a short qualitative summary. Brands in Africa often lack this data from creators. If you provide it, you become the easy choice for the next campaign.

Keep a simple CRM. Track: brand name, contact person, campaign dates, deliverables, payment status, and next follow-up date. A spreadsheet is enough. The goal is to follow up 30 days after a campaign with a new idea, not a generic âchecking inâ message.

Table 2: Payment terms and risk by African market (indicative, 2024)
Market Typical payment terms Common risk Mitigation
Kenya 50% deposit, 50% on delivery; 14â30 days Delayed payment after delivery Invoice with PO number; follow up at 7 days
Nigeria 30â60 days; often no deposit Currency fluctuation, delayed approvals Quote in USD or add FX clause; request 50% upfront
South Africa 30 days from invoice; some agencies 45â60 days Agency middleman delays Contract with agency, not just brand; confirm payment chain
Ghana 50% deposit, 50% on delivery; 14â30 days Smaller budgets, scope creep Fixed scope in contract; charge for extras

Sources: Creator community surveys and agency payment terms published by Influencer Marketing Africa and the Interactive Advertising Bureau South Africa (2023â2024). Terms vary by brand size and relationship.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Vet before you pitch: Confirm budget, niche fit, reputation, and willingness to sign a contract.
  2. Know your numbers: Have a written rate card with base fees, usage rights, and exclusivity pricing.
  3. Never sign unlimited rights: Price perpetual or worldwide usage at 3â5x base fee, or refuse.
  4. Cap exclusivity: Keep it under 90 days and narrow the category. Price it at 30â100% of base fee.
  5. Get a deposit: Aim for 50% upfront, especially with new brands or agencies.
  6. Define deliverables precisely: Platform, format, duration, posting window, and revision rounds.
  7. Report results within 72 hours: Send reach, engagement, clicks, and a short summary.
  8. Follow up in 30 days: Pitch a new idea, not a generic check-in. Repeat business is the goal.

Further Reading

  • International Trade Centre (ITC) â SME influencer marketing and digital trade resources
  • Interactive Advertising Bureau South Africa (IAB SA) â industry standards and measurement guidelines
  • Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC), South Africa â verify brand registration
  • Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), Nigeria â company verification and compliance
  • Business Registration Service (BRS), Kenya â business registration and verification

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Business-first. Africa-focused. Practical.

quiz.q: Which tool can help you find brands already working with influencers in your niche?
quiz.explanation: BuzzSumo is a content research tool that shows which brands are active with influencer campaigns.

quiz.q: What is a red flag when vetting a brand partner?
options: A) They ask for free content for exposure
B) They have a clear product
quiz.explanation: Asking for free content is a common sign that the brand does not value your work or have a budget.

quiz.q: Where can you get honest feedback about a brand's payment history?
quiz.explanation: Creator communities on WhatsApp or Twitter often share real experiences about brands.

quiz.q: What should you do before agreeing to a partnership?
quiz.explanation: A discovery call helps you clarify budget, timeline, and expectations before committing.

quiz.q: What is the ideal length for a pitch deck?
quiz.explanation: A concise 8-10 slide deck is easy to review and keeps the brand's attention.

quiz.q: Which slide should show your audience demographics?
quiz.explanation: Slide 2 typically covers audience data like age, location, and gender.

quiz.q: What file format should you send your pitch deck in?
quiz.explanation: PDF preserves formatting and is easy to open on any device.

quiz.q: What is a good formula for pricing a single post based on followers?
quiz.explanation: A common range in Africa is $50-$150 per 10k followers, depending on niche and platform.

quiz.q: If a brand wants to use your content as a paid ad for 3 months, what should you add?
quiz.explanation: Usage rights for paid ads typically add 50% to your base rate.

quiz.q: What is a common payment term for new brands?
quiz.explanation: For new brands, it's safest to require full payment upfront or at least 50%.

quiz.q: Which mobile money service is common in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa is widely used in Kenya for mobile payments.

quiz.q: What should you do if a brand offers only product and no cash?
options: B) Calculate the product's retail value
quiz.explanation: You need to assess if the product's value matches your time and usual rate.

quiz.q: What is the 'good, better, best' tactic?
options: D) Posting three times a day
quiz.explanation: It gives the brand choices and anchors the negotiation on your preferred package.

quiz.q: If a brand's budget is fixed at $80 and your rate is $150, what can you do?
quiz.explanation: You can offer a smaller deliverable, like one Story instead of a Reel, to match their budget.

quiz.q: What is anchoring in negotiation?
options: A) Starting with a high price
B) Starting with a low price
quiz.explanation: Anchoring high gives you room to negotiate down to your target rate.

quiz.q: What should you never do during negotiation?
options: A) Lower your price without getting something in return
quiz.explanation: Conceding without a trade-off devalues your work and sets a bad precedent.

quiz.q: What does an exclusivity clause mean?
options: A) You cannot work with competing brands for a period
quiz.explanation: Exclusivity restricts you from promoting competitors, usually for a set time.

quiz.q: What is a morality clause?
options: A) You won't do anything embarrassing to the brand
C) The brand pays you more
quiz.explanation: It prevents you from engaging in behaviour that could damage the brand's reputation.

quiz.q: What does 'perpetual usage worldwide' mean?
options: A) The brand can use your content forever, anywhere
C) The brand uses it for one year
quiz.explanation: Perpetual worldwide usage means the brand has unlimited rights to your content.

quiz.q: What should you do if a brand sends a 20-page contract?
options: A) Read it carefully or ask a lawyer
D) Ask for a shorter one
quiz.explanation: Always understand what you're signing; a lawyer can help spot unfair terms.

quiz.q: What is a good payment term for African creators?
quiz.explanation: Shorter payment terms like net 7 or 14 help you get paid faster.

quiz.q: What should you send within 24 hours after delivering a campaign?
options: A) A thank-you message and performance report
quiz.explanation: This shows professionalism and keeps the brand engaged for future work.

quiz.q: How often should you check in with a past brand?
quiz.explanation: Regular, non-pitch check-ins keep you top of mind without being pushy.

quiz.q: What is a loyalty program for repeat clients?
quiz.explanation: Offering a discount or extra deliverable rewards repeat business and builds loyalty.

quiz.q: Why is relationship-building important in African influencer marketing?
options: A) Word travels fast in tight-knit communities
quiz.explanation: Personal connections and reputation can make or break future deals in Africa's creator scene.

quiz.q: What should you do when you get a repeat deal?
options: A) Send a fresh contract and invoice
quiz.explanation: Each campaign should have its own contract and invoice to avoid confusion.

quiz.q: How much should you raise your rates after 6 months with a brand?
quiz.explanation: A modest increase reflects your growing value and is usually acceptable.

quiz.q: What is a good way to get more brand deals?
options: A) Ask happy clients for referrals
quiz.explanation: Referrals from satisfied clients are the most effective way to get new business.

quiz.q: What should you do if a campaign didn't go well?
quiz.explanation: Maintaining professionalism preserves your reputation and future opportunities.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of using a rate card?
options: A) It stops you from undervaluing yourself
B) It makes you look expensive
D) It's only for big influencers
quiz.explanation: A rate card sets clear standards and prevents you from accepting low offers.
